samples.question: The picture shows six separate solid horizontal bars on a plain background. Two of them are drawn in one colour and are the reference bars: one of these sits alone near the top-left corner of the page and the other sits alone near the bottom-right corner. The remaining four bars are drawn in a second colour and are stacked one above another in a single column near the middle of the page; counting downwards from the top of that column they are the first, second, third and fourth candidate bars. The length of a bar is how far it reaches from its left end to its right end. Every bar is horizontal and every bar has the same thickness, so lengths can be compared directly and thickness carries no information. Exactly one candidate bar is exactly as long as the two reference bars laid end to end, that is, as long as the length of the top-left reference bar plus the length of the bottom-right reference bar. Both reference bars are needed: each of the other three candidate bars differs from that combined length by a clearly visible amount, and one of them is built to match a single reference bar on its own, or that same single reference bar counted twice, so looking at only one corner of the page will point at the wrong bar. The colours used, which corner holds which reference bar, how long the winning bar is, where the column sits on the page, the order of the three losing bars and the isolated specks scattered in the background all carry no information. Which candidate bar in the column is exactly as long as the two reference bars added together? Answer with one of: first, second, third, fourth.
